title: LinkedHashMap: Insertion/Access Order & LRU Caches
summary: Master LinkedHashMap's dual modes: insertion-order and access-order. Build a production-grade Least-Recently-Used (LRU) cache using removeEldestEntry().
learningObjectives: Understand the dual pointer architecture of java.util.LinkedHashMap
Implement an in-memory Least-Recently-Used (LRU) cache using removeEldestEntry()
Analyze memory overhead and cache replacement performance
expectedOutcomes: Ability to design robust, self-evicting in-memory caches without external dependencies
Mastery of LinkedHashMap access-order semantics in high-performance Java applications

activities.title: Practical Context: Library Books on a High-Demand Reading Desk

analogy.headline: Practical Context: Library Books on a High-Demand Reading Desk
analogy.story:
Imagine a university research desk that holds at most 5 books. When a student requests a book, a librarian retrieves it from the shelves and places it at the rightmost end of the desk (most recently used).

Whenever a student reads or consults any book already on the desk, the librarian slides that book back to the rightmost end. If a new book arrives when the desk is full, the librarian removes the book sitting at the far left (the least recently consulted book) to make room.

This is the exact operating principle of an LRU (Least Recently Used) cache powered by LinkedHashMap in access-order mode.
analogy.keyTakeaway: LinkedHashMap in access-order mode moves accessed elements to the tail, making the head of the list the natural candidate for eviction.

activities.title: LinkedHashMap Architecture: Access-Order & In-Memory LRU Caches

keyTakeaways: LinkedHashMap extends HashMap, connecting entries with before and after pointers
Default mode is insertion-order; setting accessOrder=true activates LRU tracking
In access-order mode, invoking get() or put() shifts the accessed entry to the tail
Overriding removeEldestEntry(Map.Entry) transforms the map into an automatic self-evicting cache

activities.title: Thread-Safe Bounded Database Query Cache
activities.description: Trace a production database query cache leveraging synchronized access-order LinkedHashMap with eviction logging.

steps.description: Create an anonymous subclass of LinkedHashMap with accessOrder=true and override removeEldestEntry to evict when size > capacity.
Wrap in Collections.synchronizedMap() because access-order LinkedHashMap mutates internal pointers during get() operations, requiring thread safety.
Demonstrate that accessing users makes orders the least recently used, causing orders to be cleanly evicted when products is inserted.

questions.question: What happens when map.get(key) is invoked on a LinkedHashMap initialized with accessOrder = true?
options: Nothing; get() is strictly read-only and changes nothing
The entry corresponding to the key is moved to the tail (end) of the doubly-linked list
The entry is moved to the head of the list
questions.explanation: In access-order mode, accessing an entry via get() marks it as most-recently-used by re-linking it to the tail of the list.

questions.question: Why is an access-order LinkedHashMap not thread-safe for concurrent read operations?
options: Because read operations execute in O(N) time
Because get() mutates the internal doubly-linked list pointers to reorder nodes, causing race conditions during simultaneous reads
Because memory is cleared during concurrent reads
questions.explanation: Even though get() is conceptually a read operation, in access-order mode it writes to before/after pointers. Concurrent gets can corrupt pointers without synchronization.

questions.question: How do you enable automatic eviction of the least-recently used entry in LinkedHashMap?
options: By setting the capacity to a negative number
By overriding the protected boolean removeEldestEntry(Map.Entry eldest) method to return true when size() exceeds maximum capacity
questions.explanation: removeEldestEntry() is called by put() and putAll(). If it returns true, the eldest entry (the head) is automatically removed.

questions.question: What is the memory overhead of LinkedHashMap compared to HashMap?
options: Two additional reference pointers (before and after) per entry node
questions.explanation: LinkedHashMap.Entry subclasses HashMap.Node and adds two references: before and after, chaining all entries into a doubly-linked list.

questions.question: How would you implement an in-memory LRU Cache in Java in under 10 lines of code?
questions.answer: By subclassing LinkedHashMap: `public class LruCache<K, V> extends LinkedHashMap<K, V> { private final int max; public LruCache(int max) { super(max, 0.75f, true); this.max = max; } @Override protected boolean removeEldestEntry(Map.Entry<K, V> e) { return size() > max; } }`. Setting accessOrder to true ensures entries accessed via get/put are shifted to the tail, while removeEldestEntry evicts the head whenever the size exceeds max.

questions.question: Why is Collections.synchronizedMap(lruCache) required in concurrent web services instead of ConcurrentHashMap?
questions.answer: ConcurrentHashMap does not maintain doubly-linked insertion or access order; it has no built-in LRU support. While LinkedHashMap provides LRU mechanics, its get() method is state-mutating (reordering before/after pointers). Without synchronizing the entire access-order LinkedHashMap instance via Collections.synchronizedMap() or an explicit ReentrantLock, concurrent reads will corrupt node pointers and throw ConcurrentModificationException or cause infinite loops.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of put, get, and eviction in an LRU cache built with LinkedHashMap?
questions.answer: All three operations run in O(1) constant time on average. Key lookup in the hash table takes O(1) time. Moving an accessed node to the tail of a doubly-linked list takes O(1) pointer updates. Evicting the eldest entry from the head of the doubly-linked list and removing it from the bucket table takes O(1) time.

activities.title: Self-Evaluation: LinkedHashMap & LRU
checklist: I understand the difference between insertion-order and access-order in LinkedHashMap
I can implement a production-grade LRU cache by overriding removeEldestEntry()
I understand why get() in access-order mode is a mutating operation requiring synchronization in multithreaded environments

practiceProblems.title: Implement Fixed-Size LRU Cache
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Implement a class BoundedCache<K, V> that extends LinkedHashMap<K, V> and automatically evicts the least recently used element when size() > capacity.

testCases.expected: containsKey(2) is false, containsKey(1) is true

hints: Pass true for accessOrder in super(capacity, 0.75f, true).

practiceProblems.title: Verify Access Order Movement
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Given an access-order LinkedHashMap with items 'A', 'B', 'C', call get('A') and return a List of keys in current iteration order.
hints: Use super constructor with accessOrder = true.
Calling map.get('A') moves A to the end of the iteration order.

practiceProblems.title: Preserve Form Field Submission Order
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Write a method storeFormFields(String[][] fields) that returns a LinkedHashMap preserving the exact order in which fields were submitted.
hints: Iterate through pairs and put into map.

practiceProblems.title: Find Eldest Key Without Evicting
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Given a LinkedHashMap, return the eldest key (the first key in iteration order) without removing it, or null if the map is empty.
hints: In LinkedHashMap, the iterator starts at the eldest entry.
map.keySet().iterator().next() returns the first element in O(1) time.

practiceProblems.title: Eviction Counter Cache
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Create a class EvictionTrackingCache<K, V> extending LinkedHashMap that counts how many total entries have been evicted via removeEldestEntry.
hints: In removeEldestEntry, check if size() > capacity.
